flashcards.q: What is Resilience4j's fixed AOP decorator order for stacked annotations, and does annotation position on the method affect it?
flashcards.a: Retry(CircuitBreaker(RateLimiter(TimeLimiter(Bulkhead(Method))))) -- hardcoded by the library. Annotation declaration order on the method has no effect; override only via resilience4j.<module>.<module>AspectOrder properties.

flashcards.q: Is Resilience4j's RateLimiter a token bucket? What's the actual algorithm and its consequence?
flashcards.a: No -- fixed window. limitForPeriod permissions reset at the START of each limitRefreshPeriod cycle (tracked via lock-free AtomicReference CAS in AtomicRateLimiter). Consequence: a full burst at the end of one cycle plus a full burst at the start of the next can produce up to ~2x the nominal rate in a short boundary window.

flashcards.q: What are the two Resilience4j Bulkhead implementations, and when is each the right choice?
flashcards.a: SemaphoreBulkhead (default): counting semaphore, caller's own thread, cheap, CANNOT interrupt an in-flight call -- use for async/reactive code. ThreadPoolBulkhead: dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor + bounded queue, true isolation, CAN enforce a timeout on a blocking client -- use for legacy blocking SDKs you don't control.

flashcards.q: A @CircuitBreaker fallbackMethod is configured but never gets called -- the original exception propagates. What's the likely cause?
flashcards.a: fallbackMethod is resolved by reflection at startup against the exact original method signature plus a trailing Throwable/exception parameter. A signature mismatch fails registration silently -- no compile error, just a startup-log warning to check.

flashcards.q: Why does a SemaphoreBulkhead fail to protect against a stuck blocking downstream call with no timeout of its own?
flashcards.a: A semaphore can only block NEW calls from starting once permits run out -- it cannot interrupt a call already in flight. A stuck call holds its permit forever, so the bulkhead degrades slower than with no protection but doesn't actually stop the exhaustion.

flashcards.q: What specific gap in Hystrix does Resilience4j's slowCallRateThreshold/slowCallDurationThreshold close?
flashcards.a: Hystrix's failure-rate-only breaker never tripped on a downstream returning 200s slowly (e.g. 10s response times) -- 'slow success' exhausted threads exactly like failure but was invisible to the breaker. Leaving slowCallRateThreshold unconfigured in Resilience4j reproduces that same blind spot.

flashcards.q: Why did Hystrix's thread-pool-per-command default become a liability at scale, and how does Resilience4j fix it?
flashcards.a: Every dependency got its own dedicated thread pool by default -- real memory and context-switch cost multiplying with dependency count, with no opt-out. Resilience4j defaults to the cheap SemaphoreBulkhead and makes ThreadPoolBulkhead opt-in per dependency instead of mandatory for all.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't a synchronized-based rate limiter risk virtual thread pinning matter for Resilience4j's default RateLimiter?
flashcards.a: AtomicRateLimiter uses a lock-free AtomicReference compare-and-swap, not a synchronized block -- there's no monitor to pin a virtual thread on, regardless of JDK version.

flashcards.q: If both a service mesh and Resilience4j's @Retry are configured to retry the same call 3 times each, what happens?
flashcards.a: Amplification multiplies: up to 3x3=9 total attempts for one logical call. Pick one layer to own retry for a given call path and explicitly disable it at the other.

flashcards.q: Does Resilience4j's TimeLimiter guarantee the downstream work actually stops when it cancels a call?
flashcards.a: No -- it cancels the Future/reactive chain your code is waiting on, but the underlying downstream work only actually stops if the client itself honors thread interruption/cancellation propagation. Same server-work-continues-after-client-gives-up gap as the general resilience catalogue.
